taxonomyNote: NatureServe's English name is Sonoran mountain kingsnake; per Burbrink et al. (2011) L. pyromelana (as circumscribed by Stebbins 2003) comprises northern L. pyromelana and southern L. knoblochi.
fieldMarks: Medium-sized snake with red, white and black bands and a flat, wide head (NDOW).
Non-venomous; its red, white and black coloration mimics a coral snake (NDOW).
behavior: Mostly active by day; hides among rocks, logs and vegetation to avoid heat and predators (NDOW).
Constrictor that eats lizards, frogs, snakes, small mammals and even rattlesnakes (NDOW; NatureServe).
In Arizona adults and hatchlings were most often encountered in July and August (NatureServe).
Females lay 3-6 eggs; inactive in cold and extreme heat (NDOW; NatureServe).
habitat: Rocky, montane country often near streams or springs, also mesic lower canyons; pinyon-juniper, oak-juniper, pine-oak or pine-Douglas-fir woodland or chaparral (NatureServe; NDOW).
range: Discontinuous from east-central Nevada and central and western Utah south to near (mostly north of) the Mogollon Rim in Arizona and New Mexico (NatureServe); in Nevada limited to east-central mountains (NDOW).

lookalikes.name: Coral snakes
lookalikes.howToTell: US coral snakes have the pattern red-yellow or white-black-yellow or white-red with thin pale bands, with red and black about equal in width (CPW).
